title: Genesis 21 — The birth of Yitzchaq, the expulsion of Hagar and Yishma'el, and the covenant at Be'er Sheva

verdicts.reasoning: Standard ASV-baseline rendering of va-YHWH paqad et-Sarah. The verb paqad in the sense 'visit, attend to, take note of' is the canonical patriarchal usage (BDB 823-824; HALOT iii.955-958; Sarna JPS Genesis p. 145). No divergence from consensus.
Defensible rendering. La-moed (at the appointed time) preserved per ASV. Elohim transliteration consistent with project-wide convention (elohim-as-translation entry, claim_type direct).
Yitzchaq transliteration preserves the laughter-name-play (per yitzchaq-name-etymology-laughter-pattern entry). ASV-baseline structure preserved.
Standard rendering of the brit-milah follow-through at the eighth-day mark commanded at Gen 17:12. Both glossary refs (elohim-as-translation, brit-milah-circumcision-covenant) correctly applied.
ASV-baseline preserved verbatim.

The joy-resolution reading (kol ha-shomea yitzchaq-li as 'laugh with me') is the modern critical default. The commentary correctly documents the minor mocking-Sarah alternative (with rabbinic-tradition support) but adopts the joy-reading as ASV-baseline. Verb-and-name cluster preserved through transliteration (Yitzchaq) where Anglicized 'Isaac' would obscure the play. Defensible.

Standard ASV-baseline rendering of Sarah's rhetorical question (mi millel — who would have said). The verb millel (piel of m-l-l, to utter) is a poetic/archaic synonym for dabber (BDB 576; HALOT ii.593) — its rarity is editorially noted but not load-bearing for this verse's English.
Standard rendering of the weaning-feast event. The verb gamal (to wean) is grammatically explicit (Sarna JPS Genesis p. 146).

citations: Alter Five Books of Moses 2004, pp. 103-104
verdicts.reasoning: The translation choice 'playing' moves from ASV's 'mocking' and is defended by the modern critical consensus (Sarna, Alter, NJPS, Westermann). Independently verified against MT: metzacheq is a piel participle of tzachaq with no explicit object in the Hebrew (the LXX 'with Isaac' is expansion). The choice is editorially load-bearing on the Hagar-Yishma'el characterization but is the modern critical default and is grounded in (i) the lexical default of tzachaq, (ii) the chapter's running tz-ch-q name-play, (iii) absence of harsher direct object in MT, (iv) the editorial principle not to import rabbinic-tradition harshness on Yishma'el where the MT does not carry it. All four readings (Sarna/Alter/NJPS playing; LXX/NRSV playing-with-Isaac; ASV/KJV mocking; rabbinic-tradition maximal at Gen Rab 53:11, b. Sotah 26b, Rashi, with Pauline reception at Gal 4:29) presented in parallel in the glossary entry. Defensible at the highest scholarly bar.

Standard ASV-baseline rendering of Sarah's expulsion-demand. The amah / ben-ha-amah (handmaid / son of the handmaid) lexeme is the legal-status designator (BDB 51; HALOT i.61); ASV's 'handmaid' is preserved.
Standard rendering. The va-yera (it was grievous, qal of r-ʿ-ʿ with b-einei) idiom is the canonical disapproval-formula (Sarna JPS Genesis p. 146); ASV preserved.

Standard rendering. Elohim is grammatically explicit at the divine speech-introduction (the chapter's second-Hagar-scene Elohim-cluster, consistent with the source-critical reading documented in malakh-elohim-messenger). Defensible.
Standard ASV-baseline rendering of the Yishma'el-nation promise. Asimennu (qal imperfect 1cs of s-y-m with 3ms suffix) is grammatically explicit; ASV preserved.

citations: Alter Five Books of Moses 2004, p. 104
verdicts.reasoning: Translation modernized from ASV's 'bottle' to 'a skin of water' — defensible and matches NRSV/NJPS/Alter. The chemet (H2573) is securely identified as a leather water-skin (BDB 332; HALOT i.328), so the ASV 'bottle' is misleading in modern English. The va-teta (and she wandered) of the t-ʿ-h root is the wilderness-wandering register; rendered standardly. Editor correctly placed this lexical decision in commentary rather than in a glossary entry (appropriate for a minor non-load-bearing lexeme).
Standard ASV-baseline rendering. Va-tashlekh (and she cast/threw) is hiphil of sh-l-kh; ASV's 'cast' preserved without softening (NJPS 'left' softens the verb). Defensible.

Standard rendering of Hagar's distance-and-weeping vigil. Ki-m-tachavei qeshet (as it were a bowshot) is rendered idiomatically per ASV; Sarna JPS Genesis p. 147 notes the unusual idiom but does not propose a divergent rendering.

citations: Friedman Who Wrote the Bible? 1987, pp. 246-258
verdicts.reasoning: Independently re-parsed from MT: confirmed mal'akh Elohim (NOT mal'akh YHWH) at v 17. The translation 'the messenger of Elohim called to Hagar out of heaven' is editorially load-bearing — it preserves both the lexical etymology of mal'akh (against ASV/KJV/NRSV 'angel') and the divine-name distinction from mal'akh YHWH (Gen 16). The chapter's second-Hagar-scene Elohim-cluster (vv 12, 17 twice, 19, 20) is grammatically explicit and supports the source-critical doublet-reading documented in the malakh-elohim-messenger glossary entry. The min ha-shamayim (from heaven) qualifier and the E-document mediation-pattern (Gen 20:3 dream; Gen 28:12; Gen 31:11) are correctly cross-referenced. Defensible at the highest scholarly bar.

The paqach-et-eyneha idiom is the revelatory-perception register; the modern critical default reads the well as pre-existing and revealed to Hagar's now-opened sight, consistent with cross-corpus pattern (Num 22:31, 2 Kgs 6:17, 6:20). paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר שָׂרָ֔ה צְחֹ֕ק עָ֥שָׂה לִ֖י אֱלֹהִ֑ים כָּל־הַשֹּׁמֵ֖עַ יִֽצְחַק־לִֽי׃

i18n.en: And Sarah said, Elohim has made me to laugh; everyone that hears will laugh with me.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Tzachoq asah li Elohim kol ha-shomea yitzchaq-li* — the third and resolving instance of the Avraham-cycle's three-part laughter-Isaac play. Where Avraham's laugh at Gen 17:17 (*va-yitzchaq*) and Sarah's laugh at Gen 18:12-15 (*va-titzchaq Sarah b-qirbah*) were both internal disbelief-laughs at the announcement of conception, the v 6 laugh is the post-conception joy-laugh that closes the pattern. The verse compresses the densest verb-noun cluster of the *tz-ch-q* root in the entire chapter: the noun *tzachoq* (laughter) + the qal participle *ha-shomea* (the one who hears) + the qal imperfect *yitzchaq* (will laugh), with the name *Yitzchaq* itself naming the son.

The closing clause *kol ha-shomea yitzchaq-li* admits two readings: (i) *everyone who hears will laugh with me* (the joy-resolution reading; ASV, NJPS, Alter, Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989, p. 146) — the standard modern critical default, reading the laughter as shared joy; (ii) *everyone who hears will laugh at me* (the mocking-Sarah reading; minority position with some rabbinic support) — the laughter as derisive. The WoH translation adopts the joy-resolution reading (ASV-baseline preserved), consistent with the chapter's three-part disbelief-to-joy inversion documented in the [yitzchaq-name-etymology-laughter-pattern](#yitzchaq-name-etymology-laughter-pattern) glossary entry.

The verse's name-and-verb cluster makes the etymology of *Yitzchaq* visible in a way that conventional English (*Isaac*) cannot reproduce; the transliteration preserves the play. Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985, pp. 333-336.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֗אמֶר מִ֤י מִלֵּל֙ לְאַבְרָהָ֔ם הֵינִ֥יקָה בָנִ֖ים שָׂרָ֑ה כִּֽי־יָלַ֥דְתִּי בֵ֖ן לִזְקֻנָֽיו׃

i18n.en: And she said, Who would have said to Avraham that Sarah should nurse children? For I have borne him a son in his old age.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּגְדַּ֥ל הַיֶּ֖לֶד וַיִּגָּמַ֑ל וַיַּ֤עַשׂ אַבְרָהָם֙ מִשְׁתֶּ֣ה גָד֔וֹל בְּי֖וֹם הִגָּמֵ֥ל אֶת־יִצְחָֽק׃

i18n.en: And the child grew, and was weaned; and Avraham made a great feast on the day that Yitzchaq was weaned.

paragraphs.text: וַתֵּ֨רֶא שָׂרָ֜ה אֶֽת־בֶּן־הָגָ֧ר הַמִּצְרִ֛ית אֲשֶׁר־יָלְדָ֥ה לְאַבְרָהָ֖ם מְצַחֵֽק׃

i18n.en: And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Avraham, playing.

paragraphs.commentary:
The piel participle *metzacheq* is one of the most editorially contested verbs in the Avraham cycle, with four parallel readings each defended in the philological literature: (a) *playing / sporting* (the lexical default; Sarna, Alter, NJPS, Westermann); (b) *playing-with-Isaac* (the LXX expansion *meta Isaak tou huiou autēs*, followed by Vulgate, Peshitta, NRSV, and presupposed in Paul's *diōkōn* at Gal 4:29); (c) *mocking / abusing* (ASV/KJV, drawing on the piel's harsher uses at Gen 19:14, Gen 39:14-17, Exod 32:6); (d) the rabbinic-tradition maximal reading of *idolatry / sexual immorality / bloodshed* (Genesis Rabbah 53:11; b. Sotah 26b; Rashi). The WoH translation moves from ASV's *mocking* to *playing*, adopting the modern critical consensus default and reading the participle as the deliberate continuation of the chapter's *tzachoq* / *yitzchaq* / *Yitzchaq* name-and-verb play at vv 6-8.

The verse's syntax foregrounds Sarah's *perception* of the act, not its objective content: *and Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian ... playing*. Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985, pp. 338-339 reads the verb's semantic ambiguity as deliberate construction — the reader is left, like Avraham at v 11, uncertain how to weigh Sarah's reaction. The harsher readings are documented in the [metzacheq-ishmael-debate](#metzacheq-ishmael-debate) glossary entry but not adopted; the editorial principle is to not import rabbinic-tradition harshness on Yishma'el where the MT does not itself carry it. Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989, p. 146; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004, pp. 103-104; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995, pp. 78-79.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֙אמֶר֙ לְאַבְרָהָ֔ם גָּרֵ֛שׁ הָאָמָ֥ה הַזֹּ֖את וְאֶת־בְּנָ֑הּ כִּ֣י לֹ֤א יִירַשׁ֙ בֶּן־הָאָמָ֣ה הַזֹּ֔את עִם־בְּנִ֖י עִם־יִצְחָֽק׃

i18n.en: And she said to Avraham, Cast out this handmaid and her son: for the son of this handmaid shall not be heir with my son, with Yitzchaq.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּ֧רַע הַדָּבָ֛ר מְאֹ֖ד בְּעֵינֵ֣י אַבְרָהָ֑ם עַ֖ל אוֹדֹ֥ת בְּנֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And the thing was very grievous in Avraham's eyes on account of his son.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֜ים אֶל־אַבְרָהָ֗ם אַל־יֵרַ֤ע בְּעֵינֶ֙יךָ֙ עַל־הַנַּ֣עַר וְעַל־אֲמָתֶ֔ךָ כֹּל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר תֹּאמַ֥ר אֵלֶ֛יךָ שָׂרָ֖ה שְׁמַ֣ע בְּקֹלָ֑הּ כִּ֣י בְיִצְחָ֔ק יִקָּרֵ֥א לְךָ֖ זָֽרַע׃

i18n.en: And Elohim said to Avraham, Let it not be grievous in your eyes because of the lad, and because of your handmaid; in all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice; for in Yitzchaq shall your seed be called.

paragraphs.text: וְגַ֥ם אֶת־בֶּן־הָאָמָ֖ה לְג֣וֹי אֲשִׂימֶ֑נּוּ כִּ֥י זַרְעֲךָ֖ הֽוּא׃

i18n.en: And also of the son of the handmaid will I make a nation, because he is your seed.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֣ם אַבְרָהָ֣ם ׀ בַּבֹּ֡קֶר וַיִּֽקַּֽח־לֶחֶם֩ וְחֵ֨מַת מַ֜יִם וַיִּתֵּ֣ן אֶל־הָ֠גָר שָׂ֧ם עַל־שִׁכְמָ֛הּ וְאֶת־הַיֶּ֖לֶד וַֽיְשַׁלְּחֶ֑הָ וַתֵּ֣לֶךְ וַתֵּ֔תַע בְּמִדְבַּ֖ר בְּאֵ֥ר שָֽׁבַע׃

i18n.en: And Avraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread and a skin of water, and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away; and she departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Be'er Sheva.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Chemat mayim* — the *chemet* (חֵמֶת, H2573) is a leather water-skin, the load-bearing object of the expulsion scene and the chapter's three-verse arc (v 14 *chemat mayim* — *a skin of water*; v 15 *va-yikhlu ha-mayim min ha-chemet* — *the water was spent from the skin*; v 19 *va-tmaleh et ha-chemet mayim* — *she filled the skin with water*). The lexeme is a hapax-cluster in Genesis (recurring only at Hab 2:15 in the rest of the HB). ASV's *bottle* (KJV/RSV) is now misleading in modern English where *bottle* suggests a glass-or-plastic vessel; NRSV / NJPS / Alter render *skin / waterskin*, closer to the leather-vessel ANE reality. The WoH translation reads *a skin of water*, preserving the modernized lexeme without committing it to its own glossary entry (a minor lexical decision, recorded in commentary).

The geographical placement *b-midbar Be'er Sheva* (*in the wilderness of Be'er Sheva*) marks the chapter's first Be'er-Sheva reference and anticipates the v 31 in-text etiology of the place-name (see [be-er-sheva-folk-etymology](#be-er-sheva-folk-etymology) for the double-etymology *sheva*-as-seven / *shava*-as-oath). The wandering-in-the-wilderness register (*va-tetа* — *and she wandered*; the verb *t-ʿ-h*) anticipates the deeper expulsion-and-rescue narrative that the *paqach Elohim et eyneha* of v 19 will resolve.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּכְל֥וּ הַמַּ֖יִם מִן־הַחֵ֑מֶת וַתַּשְׁלֵ֣ךְ אֶת־הַיֶּ֔לֶד תַּ֖חַת אַחַ֥ד הַשִּׂיחִֽם׃

i18n.en: And the water in the skin was spent, and she cast the child under one of the shrubs.

paragraphs.text: וַתֵּלֶךְ֩ וַתֵּ֨שֶׁב לָ֜הּ מִנֶּ֗גֶד הַרְחֵק֙ כִּמְטַחֲוֵ֣י קֶ֔שֶׁת כִּ֣י אָֽמְרָ֔ה אַל־אֶרְאֶ֖ה בְּמ֣וֹת הַיָּ֑לֶד וַתֵּ֣שֶׁב מִנֶּ֔גֶד וַתִּשָּׂ֥א אֶת־קֹלָ֖הּ וַתֵּֽבְךְּ׃

i18n.en: And she went, and sat down opposite him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child. And she sat opposite him, and lifted up her voice, and wept.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁמַ֣ע אֱלֹהִים֮ אֶת־ק֣וֹל הַנַּעַר֒ וַיִּקְרָא֩ מַלְאַ֨ךְ אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ אֶל־הָגָר֙ מִן־הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לָ֖הּ מַה־לָּ֣ךְ הָגָ֑ר אַל־תִּ֣ירְאִ֔י כִּֽי־שָׁמַ֧ע אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶל־ק֥וֹל הַנַּ֖עַר בַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר הוּא־שָֽׁם׃

i18n.en: And Elohim heard the voice of the lad; and the messenger of Elohim called to Hagar out of heaven, and said to her, What ails you, Hagar? Fear not; for Elohim has heard the voice of the lad where he is.

paragraphs.commentary:
The verse contains the first Hebrew Bible occurrence of *mal'akh Elohim* — *messenger of Elohim* — and is editorially distinct from the *mal'akh YHWH* of the first Hagar-scene at Gen 16:7-13. The chapter's second Hagar-scene (vv 14-21) uses *Elohim* consistently throughout (vv 12, 17 twice, 19, 20) where Gen 16 used *YHWH* and *mal'akh YHWH* throughout. The divine-name register is consistently different across the two Hagar-scenes.

Modern critical scholarship reads the divine-name shift as the principal source-critical evidence for the documentary attribution of the two Hagar-scenes to different sources: Gen 16 to the **J-document** (the Yahwist), Gen 21:8-21 to the **E-document** (the Elohist), with the two scenes constituting a *doublet* — the same basic narrative (Hagar in the wilderness, divine encounter at a well, promise of Yishma'el's tribal future) attested in two parallel source-versions. Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985, pp. 339-340; Speiser *Anchor Bible Genesis* 1964, pp. 155-157; Friedman *Who Wrote the Bible?* 1987, pp. 246-258; Skinner *ICC Genesis* 1910, pp. 320-325. The post-documentary critique (Van Seters 1975, Carr 1996, Schmid 1999) preserves the doublet-recognition while questioning the four-source attribution; the source-critical reading is the standard modern-critical treatment without being uniquely consensus.

The *min ha-shamayim* (from heaven) qualifier marks a remoter mode of encounter than Gen 16's wilderness messenger who is *found* by Hagar at the spring and identified as YHWH at v 13. The Gen 21 messenger *calls* from heaven and is not physically present; the well of v 19 is revealed only by Elohim's opening of Hagar's eyes. The mediated-immanence register is consistent with the E-document's broader pattern (Gen 20:3 the dream-revelation to Avimelekh; Gen 28:12 the *mal'akhei Elohim* on the ladder; Gen 31:11 the *mal'akh ha-Elohim* in Ya'aqov's dream). See [malakh-elohim-messenger](#malakh-elohim-messenger) for the full source-critical and cross-corpus treatment.

paragraphs.text: ק֚וּמִי שְׂאִ֣י אֶת־הַנַּ֔עַר וְהַחֲזִ֥יקִי אֶת־יָדֵ֖ךְ בּ֑וֹ כִּֽי־לְג֥וֹי גָּד֖וֹל אֲשִׂימֶֽנּוּ׃

i18n.en: Arise, lift up the lad, and hold him by your hand; for I will make him a great nation.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּפְקַ֤ח אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת־עֵינֶ֔יהָ וַתֵּ֖רֶא בְּאֵ֣ר מָ֑יִם וַתֵּ֜לֶךְ וַתְּמַלֵּ֤א אֶת־הַחֵ֙מֶת֙ מַ֔יִם וַתַּ֖שְׁקְ אֶת־הַנָּֽעַר׃

i18n.en: And Elohim opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went, and filled the skin with water, and gave the lad drink.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yifqach Elohim et-eyneha va-tere be'er mayim* — the patriarchal corpus's first occurrence of the *paqach et ha-eynayim* (open the eyes) idiom in the revelatory-discovery register. The idiom names a developed Hebrew Bible figure for deity-induced perceptual revelation: a shift in the recipient's sight that brings a previously-hidden reality into view. The cross-corpus pattern is consistent: at Num 22:31 the deity uncovers Bil'am's eyes to see the *mal'akh YHWH* who had been standing in the road all along; at 2 Kgs 6:17 Elisha prays that his servant's eyes be opened to see the chariots of fire already on the mountain; at 2 Kgs 6:20 the verb operates in reverse on the Aramean army within Samaria. In every cross-corpus instance the deity opens the recipient's eyes to a reality that was already present but unseen.

The well of v 19 is editorially read in two main ways: (a) the *well-was-always-there* reading — the well is a pre-existing wilderness spring that Hagar had been unable to see; the divine action is Hagar's perception, not the well's creation. This is the modern critical default (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989, p. 147; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985, p. 343; NJPS; NRSV; Alter 2004, p. 105) and reflects the lexical core of the *paqach-eynayim* idiom across the HB. (b) The rabbinic-tradition *well-created-at-the-moment* reading (Genesis Rabbah 53:14; Pseudo-Jonathan; Midrash Tanchuma) — the well as ad hoc miracle, included in the list of created-at-twilight-of-the-sixth-day wells in the Mishnaic tradition. The WoH translation adopts the modern critical default; the rabbinic-tradition reading is documented in the [paqach-eynayim-revelatory-perception](#paqach-eynayim-revelatory-perception) glossary entry but not adopted.

Within the Avraham cycle, Hagar's pattern across the two scenes is editorially significant: at Gen 16:13 Hagar names the deity who saw her (*El Ro'i* — *the El who sees*; the first divine-name-naming by a woman in the HB); at Gen 21:19 the same deity opens her seeing. The foreign-Egyptian-woman-as-seer pattern is documented by Trible *Texts of Terror* 1984; Reis *Reading the Lines* 2002.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֧י אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶת־הַנַּ֖עַר וַיִּגְדָּ֑ל וַיֵּ֙שֶׁב֙ בַּמִּדְבָּ֔ר וַיְהִ֖י רֹבֶ֥ה קַשָּֽׁת׃

i18n.en: And Elohim was with the lad, and he grew; and he dwelt in the wilderness, and became, as he grew up, an archer.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּ֖שֶׁב בְּמִדְבַּ֣ר פָּארָ֑ן וַתִּֽקַּֽח־ל֥וֹ אִמּ֛וֹ אִשָּׁ֖ה מֵאֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And he dwelt in the wilderness of Paran; and his mother took him a wife out of the land of Mitsrayim.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִי֙ בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֔וא וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲבִימֶ֗לֶךְ וּפִיכֹל֙ שַׂר־צְבָא֔וֹ אֶל־אַבְרָהָ֖ם לֵאמֹ֑ר אֱלֹהִ֣ים עִמְּךָ֔ בְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֖ה עֹשֶֽׂה׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass at that time, that Avimelekh and Phicol the captain of his host spoke to Avraham, saying, Elohim is with you in all that you do.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Elohim imkha b-khol asher atah oseh* — the first patriarchal occurrence of the *Elohim/YHWH im-X* (Elohim/YHWH is with X) divine-presence formula, one of the most distributionally extensive recurring phrases in the Hebrew Bible. The formula names the deity's accompaniment-as-favor and serves across the corpus as the basis for inter-personal trust, treaty, and political alignment.

The verse is doubly editorially significant. First, it is the formula's first patriarchal occurrence — the inaugural deployment of what becomes the canonical HB divine-accompaniment phrase across Gen 26 (Yitzchaq), Gen 28-31 (Ya'aqov), Gen 39 (Yosef), Exod 3 (Moses), Deut 31 / Josh 1 (the Joshua-transition), and on through the Davidic narratives, the Solomonic temple-dedication, the prophetic-call inaugurations, and the post-exilic restoration material. Second, the formula appears on the lips of a *non-Israelite king* — Avimelekh of Gerar — recognizing the divine accompaniment of the patriarch from the outside. The external-recognition register is itself a developed HB pattern (the Yitzchaq doublet at Gen 26:28 uses the same formula on the same king's lips; cf. Pharaoh recognizing the *ruach Elohim* in Yosef at Gen 41:38; Bil'am recognizing YHWH's blessing of Israel at Num 22-24).

Within the chapter's structure, v 22 is the pivot from the Hagar-expulsion narrative (vv 1-21) to the Avimelekh-treaty narrative (vv 22-34). The pivot is editorially deliberate: the chapter has just demonstrated *Elohim imkha* through the Hagar-and-Yishma'el rescue (where *Elohim* appears five times across vv 12-20), and Avimelekh's recognition at v 22 is the external confirmation of the divine-accompaniment that the preceding pericope has just narratively established. H. D. Preuss *Jahweglaube und Zukunftserwartung* (BWANT 87) 1968 is the foundational monograph-treatment of the formula across the HB; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985, p. 343; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989, pp. 147-148.

paragraphs.text: וְעַתָּ֗ה הִשָּׁ֨בְעָה לִּ֤י בֵֽאלֹהִים֙ הֵ֔נָּה אִם־תִּשְׁקֹ֣ר לִ֔י וּלְנִינִ֖י וּלְנֶכְדִּ֑י כַּחֶ֜סֶד אֲשֶׁר־עָשִׂ֤יתִי עִמְּךָ֙ תַּעֲשֶׂ֣ה עִמָּדִ֔י וְעִם־הָאָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־גַּ֥רְתָּה בָּֽהּ׃

i18n.en: Now therefore swear to me here by Elohim that you will not deal falsely with me, nor with my son, nor with my son's son: but according to the kindness that I have done to you, you shall do to me, and to the land in which you have sojourned.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ אַבְרָהָ֔ם אָנֹכִ֖י אִשָּׁבֵֽעַ׃

i18n.en: And Avraham said, I will swear.

paragraphs.text: וְהוֹכִ֥חַ אַבְרָהָ֖ם אֶת־אֲבִימֶ֑לֶךְ עַל־אֹדוֹת֙ בְּאֵ֣ר הַמַּ֔יִם אֲשֶׁ֥ר גָּזְל֖וּ עַבְדֵ֥י אֲבִימֶֽלֶךְ׃

i18n.en: And Avraham reproved Avimelekh on account of the well of water, which Avimelekh's servants had violently taken away.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲבִימֶ֔לֶךְ לֹ֣א יָדַ֔עְתִּי מִ֥י עָשָׂ֖ה אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וְגַם־אַתָּ֞ה לֹא־הִגַּ֣דְתָּ לִּ֗י וְגַ֧ם אָנֹכִ֛י לֹ֥א שָׁמַ֖עְתִּי בִּלְתִּ֥י הַיּֽוֹם׃

i18n.en: And Avimelekh said, I know not who has done this thing; neither did you tell me, neither yet did I hear of it, except today.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֤ח אַבְרָהָם֙ צֹ֣אן וּבָקָ֔ר וַיִּתֵּ֖ן לַאֲבִימֶ֑לֶךְ וַיִּכְרְת֥וּ שְׁנֵיהֶ֖ם בְּרִֽית׃

i18n.en: And Avraham took sheep and oxen, and gave them to Avimelekh; and they two made a covenant.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּצֵּ֣ב אַבְרָהָ֗ם אֶת־שֶׁ֛בַע כִּבְשֹׂ֥ת הַצֹּ֖אן לְבַדְּהֶֽן׃

i18n.en: And Avraham set seven ewe-lambs of the flock by themselves.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֲבִימֶ֖לֶךְ אֶל־אַבְרָהָ֑ם מָ֣ה הֵ֗נָּה שֶׁ֤בַע כְּבָשֹׂת֙ הָאֵ֔לֶּה אֲשֶׁ֥ר הִצַּ֖בְתָּ לְבַדָּֽנָה׃

i18n.en: And Avimelekh said to Avraham, What do these seven ewe-lambs mean, which you have set by themselves?

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר כִּ֚י אֶת־שֶׁ֣בַע כְּבָשֹׂ֔ת תִּקַּ֖ח מִיָּדִ֑י בַּעֲבוּר֙ תִּֽהְיֶה־לִּ֣י לְעֵדָ֔ה כִּ֥י חָפַ֖רְתִּי אֶת־הַבְּאֵ֥ר הַזֹּֽאת׃

i18n.en: And he said, These seven ewe-lambs you shall take from my hand, that it may be a witness to me, that I have dug this well.

paragraphs.text: עַל־כֵּ֗ן קָרָ֛א לַמָּק֥וֹם הַה֖וּא בְּאֵ֣ר שָׁ֑בַע כִּ֛י שָׁ֥ם נִשְׁבְּע֖וּ שְׁנֵיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: Therefore he called that place Be'er Sheva, because there they both swore an oath.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Be'er Sheva* — the chapter's in-text etiology of the place-name. The place-name is morphologically a construct chain *be'er* (well) + *sheva*, and the second element *sheva* sustains a deliberate double-etymology on the **sh-b-ʿ** root: *sheva* (שֶׁבַע — *seven*; the seven ewe-lambs of vv 28-30 set aside as the legal witness *l-edah*) and *shava* (שָׁבַע — *to swear an oath*; *ki sham nishb'u sh'neihem* — *because there they both swore*). The two senses are not alternatives but layered: the seven-ewe-lambs are the materials of the oath-swearing, and the oath-swearing ratifies the seven-ewe-lambs arrangement. The chapter compresses both the witness-object and the witness-act into a single phonological cluster.

The parallel etiology at **Gen 26:33** activates only the *sheva*-as-oath sense (Yitzchaq's parallel-but-distinct Avimelekh covenant uses *nishb'u* / *Shiv'ah* without the seven-ewe-lambs object-arrangement), confirming the layered-vs-partial doublet structure of the two cycles. Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989, p. 149; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994, pp. 92-95; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985, pp. 348-349.

The toponym becomes the canonical southern-boundary marker of the Israelite land in the *Dan-to-Be'er-Sheva* formula (Judg 20:1; 1 Sam 3:20; 2 Sam 3:10; etc.). The historical Be'er Sheva is securely identified with Tell es-Seba per the Aharoni 1973 / Herzog 1984/2016 excavation reports. The WoH translation preserves the transliteration *Be'er Sheva*, matching the WoH compound-place-name convention and preserving the double-etymology visibly; the Anglicized *Beer-sheba* (ASV) loses both the construct-chain structure and the *sheva* / *shava* play.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּכְרְת֥וּ בְרִ֖ית בִּבְאֵ֣ר שָׁ֑בַע וַיָּ֣קָם אֲבִימֶ֗לֶךְ וּפִיכֹל֙ שַׂר־צְבָא֔וֹ וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים׃

i18n.en: So they made a covenant at Be'er Sheva: and Avimelekh rose up, and Phicol the captain of his host, and they returned into the land of the Philistines.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּטַּ֥ע אֶ֖שֶׁל בִּבְאֵ֣ר שָׁ֑בַע וַיִּ֨קְרָא־שָׁ֔ם בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה אֵ֥ל עוֹלָֽם׃

i18n.en: And Avraham planted a tamarisk in Be'er Sheva, and there called on the name of YHWH, the Everlasting El.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yita eshel bi-Be'er Sheva va-yiqra-sham b-shem YHWH El Olam* — the chapter's keystone cultic-site verse, naming the cult-site (Be'er Sheva), the cultic-marker (the *eshel* — tamarisk), the invocation-formula (*qara b-shem YHWH*), and the divine name (*YHWH El Olam*) in a single compact verse. This is the only formal Avraham-cultic-site-establishment in the Genesis cycle that combines all four elements.

*YHWH El Olam.* The verse contains the first occurrence of *El Olam* (the Everlasting El) in the Hebrew Bible and completes the four-fold patriarchal El-compound divine-naming pattern in the Avraham cycle: **El Elyon** at Gen 14:18-22 (Avram and Melchizedek); **El Ro'i** at Gen 16:13 (Hagar at the wilderness spring); **El Shaddai** at Gen 17:1 (the covenant-of-circumcision); and now **El Olam** at Gen 21:33. The four El-compounds across four distinct sanctuary-sites stage the patriarchal religious geography as a four-fold El-cult.

The religious-historical reconstruction reads the patriarchal El-compound pattern as preserving a *West-Semitic El-religion locally diversified*, with each sanctuary-site preserving a distinct El-compound divine name corresponding to that site's pre-Israelite high-god cult. The Yahwistic editor then harmonizes each El-compound with YHWH through the appositional construction — *YHWH El Elyon* at Gen 14:22 (Avram's oath to Melchizedek), now *YHWH El Olam* at Gen 21:33 (Avraham at his own cultic-site). The reading is grounded in Alt *Der Gott der Väter* 1929 (the foundational monograph) and developed in Cross *Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic* 1973, ch. 1 (the canonical modern statement), with reinforcement from the Ugaritic textual corpus, the Deir ʿAlla inscription, the Karatepe inscription's *El qoneh ʾerets*, and Philo of Byblos' Sanchuniathon-fragment. Smith *The Origins of Biblical Monotheism* 2001; Day *Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan* 2000; Köckert 1988.

The *olam* lexeme is read in the temporal-duration register (*long duration, indefinite extent in time*) rather than the abstract-eternity register (the latter is a later semantic development; HALOT ii.798-799; BDB 761-763; TDOT vol. 10 by H. D. Preuss; Jenni 1952-53). The WoH translation preserves ASV's *Everlasting El*, rejecting the NIV-style overreading to *Eternal God* and keeping the El-compound visible by substituting *El* for the generic *God*.

*The eshel.* Avraham *plants* (*va-yita*) an *eshel* — the *Tamarix aphylla* (the leafless tamarisk, native to the Negev). The lexeme is a botanical hapax-cluster: only three Hebrew Bible occurrences (Gen 21:33; 1 Sam 22:6 Saul under the tamarisk at Gibeah; 1 Sam 31:13 Saul's bones buried under the tamarisk at Yavesh-Gilead). The Avraham-tamarisk is the only patriarchal sacred-tree-site that is *deliberately planted by the patriarch himself* rather than pre-existing — in contrast with the *elon Moreh* at Shechem (Gen 12:6), the *elonei Mamre* (Gen 13:18, 18:1), and the wider sacred-tree-cultic-marker pattern. The *plant + cult-site + invocation* arrangement at v 33 founds the site as Avraham's own cultic-marker. See [eshel-tamarisk-cultic-site](#eshel-tamarisk-cultic-site) for the sacred-tree-cultic-marker pattern across the wider HB lexeme-cluster (Pope *Song of Songs* 1985; Frevel 1995; Olyan 1988; Hadley 2000).

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֧גָר אַבְרָהָ֛ם בְּאֶ֥רֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּ֖ים יָמִ֥ים רַבִּֽים׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And Avraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines many days.
